title: The desert fathers
hookLine: in the 300s, men like Antony went into the Egyptian desert to pray and people came asking for a word

cards: A young man in Egypt has lost his parents, and they've left him land.

Not long after, he walks into church just as the Gospel is being read, the words Jesus said to a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor." He takes it personally.
He sells the land, gives the money away, and eventually walks into the desert to pray. His name is Antony. He wanted to be alone with God.
Instead, people followed him, year after year. And when they found him, they asked for one thing.

teach.b: A new stretch of the path starts here: the mystics, the Christians across the centuries who gave their whole lives to prayer. They begin in the sand.
In the 300s, men and women went out into the deserts of Egypt, Palestine and Syria. Some lived alone in caves. Some lived in loose villages of huts, gathering for worship.
The desert was no escape to comfort. It was hot, empty and hungry, and they went on purpose, to strip life down to God and the heart. The name people gave a wise old monk was abba.
You've met that word before on this path: it's the Aramaic word for father.
Jesus prayed it in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee." In the desert, it became a title of love and respect for a spiritual father.
Visitors, some from far away, would find an abba sitting outside his hut and say one simple thing: Abba, give me a word. Not a lecture. One short saying to take home and live on, maybe for years.
Those sayings were remembered and written down, and a collection of them, the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, is still read today. They're short, and some are strange or funny.

One tradition tells of Antony seeing the snares of evil spread over the whole earth and asking who could possibly get through them. The answer he heard was a single word: humility. That's the desert in miniature.
Not a system. A word, given by someone who had lived it, to someone who had walked a long way to ask.

how: Christians in Orthodox and Catholic monastic traditions, among others, still read the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and seek out a spiritual father or mother, an elder, for a word of guidance.

games.q: you've walked a long way into the desert. an old monk is sitting outside his hut. what do you ask?
games.why: that was the custom: one short word to take home and live on, sometimes for years.

practice: Think of an elder in your life, someone who has lived through more than you: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, a boss who was kind. Picture sitting with them and asking for one word, one short piece of advice.
What do you think they'd say? Hold that word.

wordCard.voice: Abba. Father, in Aramaic. The name the desert gave its wise old monks.

orig.note: Aramaic word for father, written in Greek letters; the desert's title for a wise elder.

carryVoice: Your line: give me a word. One word, lived on for years, can be enough. That's day two hundred sixty-two.
